headline: CMS Proposes RAPID Medicare Device Path
dek: The voluntary proposal would coordinate Medicare coverage reviews with FDA authorization for selected breakthrough devices, with final coverage goals of 60 or 90 days.
entities: Transitional Coverage for Emerging Technologies Program

sources.title: Medicare Program; Regulatory Alignment for Predictable and Immediate Device Coverage Pathway
RAPID coverage pathway proposed notice, official PDF

lead.creator: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
lead.rightsBasis: The FDA laboratory photograph is a work of the U.S. federal government and is identified as public domain on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.attribution: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, public domain
lead.caption: An FDA biophysics laboratory studies medical devices used with the heart. CMS has proposed a coordinated Medicare coverage pathway for selected breakthrough devices.
lead.alt: Laboratory equipment and monitors used to study cardiac medical devices.

charts.caption: The proposed pathway distinguishes participating Class II and Class III breakthrough devices and requires evidence planning with FDA and CMS.
charts.alt: Graphic summarizes proposed RAPID pathway eligibility for selected Class II and Class III breakthrough devices.

charts.caption: CMS proposes posting a coverage proposal on the FDA authorization date when evidence is sufficient, followed by different final-decision goals for Class II and Class III devices.
charts.alt: Graphic shows same-day proposed coverage followed by 60-day and 90-day final coverage goals.

paragraphs: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has proposed a voluntary pathway intended to coordinate Medicare coverage decisions with Food and Drug Administration review for selected breakthrough medical devices.

The Regulatory Alignment for Predictable and Immediate Device, or RAPID, pathway would be open to certain Class II FDA Breakthrough Devices enrolled in the Transitional Coverage for Emerging Technologies program and to Class III Breakthrough Devices whether or not they are enrolled in that program.

Participation would not make coverage automatic. A device would need to enter the pathway by the investigational-device-exemption presubmission stage, include Medicare beneficiaries in its evidence plan and study health outcomes agreed upon with FDA and CMS.

When CMS concludes that the evidence is sufficient, the agency proposes posting a national coverage determination on the same day FDA grants market authorization. CMS describes that first document as a proposed coverage determination, not the final decision.

The agency's stated goal is to issue a final national coverage determination as soon as 60 days after authorization for eligible Class II devices and 90 days after authorization for eligible Class III devices. Those are proposed goals rather than guaranteed deadlines.

The proposal is designed to let manufacturers address FDA safety-and-effectiveness questions and Medicare coverage evidence needs through a coordinated development plan. The agencies have different legal responsibilities, so FDA authorization alone would still not establish Medicare coverage.

CMS says the pathway would focus on products that can generate evidence relevant to the Medicare population. A study that does not enroll Medicare beneficiaries or measure the agreed outcomes would not satisfy the proposed evidence conditions merely because the product carries breakthrough designation.
The notice seeks public comment through Oct. 13, 2026. CMS can revise or decline the proposal after reviewing comments, and no device can use RAPID unless a final pathway is established.

For patients and clinicians, the proposal is a coverage-process change rather than a medical recommendation. Individual coverage would still depend on the final national determination, benefit rules and the circumstances of care.
facts: RAPID is a proposed voluntary pathway, not a current Medicare benefit.
Selected Class II and Class III FDA Breakthrough Devices could qualify under different conditions.
CMS proposes final coverage-decision goals of 60 days for Class II and 90 days for Class III devices.
Comments are due Oct. 13, 2026.
uncertainty: CMS may change or withdraw the proposal after public comment.
The notice does not guarantee coverage for any device or a fixed decision date.
seoTitle: CMS RAPID Medicare device coverage proposal: 60- and 90-day goals
seoDescription: CMS proposes a RAPID pathway coordinating Medicare coverage with FDA review for selected breakthrough devices, with 60- and 90-day goals.

headline: Unalaska Harbor Plan Faces Sea-Otter Review
dek: A proposed federal authorization estimates that pile work at Robert Storrs Harbor could disturb up to 112 sea otters during as many as 100 nonconsecutive workdays.

sources.title: Marine Mammals; Incidental Take During Specified Activities; Proposed Incidental Harassment Authorization
Robert Storrs Harbor proposed incidental-harassment authorization, official PDF

lead.creator: RndmCrs
lead.rightsBasis: The Alaska sea-otter photograph was dedicated to the public domain under CC0 by its creator on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: A sea otter floats in Alaska waters. Federal reviewers are considering a one-year harassment authorization tied to proposed pile work at Robert Storrs Harbor in Unalaska.
lead.alt: A sea otter floating on its back in calm Alaska water.

charts.caption: The city's plan combines removal and installation of steel piles over as many as 100 nonconsecutive pile-work days.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 33 piles to be removed, five temporary piles and 44 permanent piles.

charts.caption: Fish and Wildlife Service modeling separates harassment events from the maximum number of individual sea otters that could be affected.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 32 Level A events, 273 Level B events and up to 112 individual sea otters.

paragraphs: Federal wildlife officials are reviewing a proposed one-year authorization for pile work at Robert Storrs Harbor in Unalaska, Alaska, that the government estimates could disturb up to 112 sea otters.

The City of Unalaska plans to remove 33 steel piles, install and later remove five temporary piles, and install 44 permanent piles. The proposed notice allows for pile-related activity on as many as 100 nonconsecutive days.

Under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, the word take can include harassment. The proposal does not estimate that 112 animals would be killed; it models potential disturbance and possible injury-level exposure from construction noise.

The Fish and Wildlife Service estimates 32 instances of Level A harassment affecting 32 sea otters and 273 instances of Level B harassment affecting as many as 112 otters. Event counts can exceed the number of individual animals because the same animal may be exposed more than once.

Level A harassment covers exposure with the potential to injure a marine mammal, while Level B covers disturbance that can alter behavioral patterns. Those regulatory categories do not mean that every modeled exposure will produce an observed effect.

The service compares the maximum 112 individuals with its estimated southwest Alaska stock of 51,935 sea otters, or about 0.22%. It uses that comparison, proposed mitigation and monitoring measures to support its preliminary negligible-impact finding.

Mitigation described in the notice includes defined monitoring and shutdown zones, trained observers and work restrictions when animals enter specified areas. The final authorization could alter those conditions after public review.
The authorization would cover only the activity, period and limits described in the final record. It would not remove other federal, state or local construction requirements.
Comments are due Sept. 10, 2026. Until the Fish and Wildlife Service issues a final decision, the exposure estimates and authorization terms remain proposed.
facts: The project includes removal of 33 piles and installation of five temporary and 44 permanent piles.
Pile work could occur on up to 100 nonconsecutive days.
The proposal estimates 32 Level A and 273 Level B harassment instances affecting up to 112 sea otters.
Comments are due Sept. 10, 2026.
uncertainty: The modeled harassment estimates are not observations and do not predict a certain effect for each animal.
The service may change the proposed authorization or mitigation conditions after public comment.
seoTitle: Unalaska harbor sea-otter review estimates up to 112 animals
seoDescription: A proposed authorization for Robert Storrs Harbor pile work estimates harassment affecting up to 112 sea otters over as many as 100 workdays.

headline: USITC Orders LCD Glass Import Exclusions
dek: The commission found a Section 337 violation involving two Corning patents and issued limited relief covering infringing LCD glass products tied to four remaining respondents.

sources.title: Certain Glass Substrates for Liquid Crystal Displays, Products Containing the Same, and Methods for Manufacturing the Same
USITC LCD glass investigation termination notice, official PDF

lead.creator: Siarhei Besarab
lead.rightsBasis: The documentary photograph was released by its creator under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 license on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: A disassembled LCD screen assembly shows the layered construction of a display. The USITC order concerns specified infringing LCD glass substrates and products, not every LCD device.
lead.alt: A disassembled laptop LCD screen assembly with layers and cables visible.

charts.caption: The final notice identifies four remaining respondent groups after other companies left the investigation through settlements or earlier terminations.
charts.alt: Graphic lists Caihong, CSOT, CHOT and TCL as the four remaining respondents.

charts.caption: The commission issued a limited exclusion order and one cease-and-desist order, with a zero-percent bond during presidential review.
charts.alt: Graphic summarizes the limited exclusion order, TCL cease-and-desist order and zero-percent bond.

paragraphs: The U.S. International Trade Commission has issued a limited exclusion order covering specified infringing LCD glass substrates and related products after finding a violation of Section 337 of the Tariff Act.
The commission's Aug. 6 vote concerned remaining claims of U.S. patents 8,642,491 and 8,640,498 held by Corning. The public notice was published in the Federal Register on Tuesday.

The exclusion order applies to unlicensed infringing articles imported for four remaining respondent groups identified in the notice: Caihong, CSOT, CHOT and TCL. It is not a blanket prohibition on all LCD panels, televisions or computers.

The commission also issued a cease-and-desist order against TTE Technology, which does business as TCL North America. That order addresses specified domestic commercial conduct involving covered articles.

During the presidential review period, covered imports may enter under a bond set at zero percent of entered value. The bond rate does not cancel the exclusion order; it is the commission's term for the review period.

The investigation originally named additional respondents, including companies later removed through settlements or other terminations. Those earlier departures are distinct from the final merits determination concerning the remaining respondents.
A limited exclusion order is narrower than a general exclusion order. Its scope turns on the patent claims, the products and the respondent relationships described in the commission record.

The notice does not predict how many products will be stopped at the border or whether retail availability will change. Customs administration, licensing and product-specific infringement questions can affect the practical result.

The commission terminated the investigation after issuing the final remedial orders. Parties may pursue the review options available under federal law, but the published notice records the commission's current final action.
facts: The commission found a Section 337 violation involving two Corning patents.
A limited exclusion order covers specified infringing articles tied to four remaining respondent groups.
A cease-and-desist order applies to TTE Technology doing business as TCL North America.
The bond during presidential review is zero percent.
uncertainty: The notice does not quantify affected import volume or retail availability.
Product coverage depends on the patent claims, licensing and the order's respondent scope.
seoTitle: USITC LCD glass exclusion order covers four respondent groups
seoDescription: The USITC issued limited LCD glass import relief after finding infringement tied to Corning patents and four remaining respondent groups.

headline: EPA Sets Conditions for New Hampshire Emissions-Test Change
dek: The proposal would move vehicle emissions inspections from an active state air-plan measure to a contingency, but only if New Hampshire leaves the Ozone Transport Region.

sources.title: Air Plan Approval; New Hampshire; Repeal of Motor Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance Program
New Hampshire inspection-and-maintenance air-plan proposal, official PDF

lead.creator: Lyntha Scott Eiler / U.S. National Archives
lead.rightsBasis: The documentary emissions-inspection photograph is a U.S. federal government record and public domain.
lead.attribution: Lyntha Scott Eiler / U.S. National Archives, public domain
lead.caption: A motorist waits during an automobile emissions test in a U.S. inspection program. EPA's New Hampshire action is still a conditional proposal and does not itself end current requirements.
lead.alt: A motorist reads a brochure while a car undergoes an exhaust-emissions test.

charts.caption: New Hampshire's comparison models lower statewide emissions in 2026 without the active inspection program than in the 2022 baseline with it.
charts.alt: Graphic shows modeled changes of minus 16 percent nitrogen oxides, minus 2.7 percent volatile organic compounds and minus 1.9 percent carbon monoxide.

charts.caption: EPA's proposed approval depends on a separate Ozone Transport Region decision and a follow-up state air-plan revision within one year.
charts.alt: Graphic shows Ozone Transport Region removal, final conditional approval and a one-year follow-up deadline.

paragraphs: The Environmental Protection Agency has proposed conditionally approving New Hampshire's request to remove its motor-vehicle emissions inspection program as an active measure in the state's federally enforceable air plan.

The proposal would retain the inspection-and-maintenance program as a possible contingency measure rather than erase it from the plan entirely. It does not by itself repeal a current state inspection requirement.

EPA says final approval would depend on the agency separately granting New Hampshire's request to leave the Ozone Transport Region. Without that separate action, the condition described in Tuesday's proposal would not be satisfied.

New Hampshire would also have to submit another state implementation plan revision within one year of a final conditional approval. If it misses that commitment, the conditional approval would automatically convert to a disapproval under the Clean Air Act process described by EPA.

State modeling compares a 2022 baseline with the inspection program to projected 2026 conditions without it. The model shows nitrogen-oxide emissions down 16.0%, volatile organic compounds down 2.7% and carbon monoxide down 1.9%, even as vehicle miles traveled rise.
Those percentages are projections, not measurements of what happened after a repeal. EPA and the state attribute much of the modeled decline to turnover toward newer vehicles with lower emissions.

The federal air-plan question is also separate from New Hampshire's safety-inspection rules and any state implementation timetable. Drivers should not treat the proposal as a change to current compliance obligations.
EPA is asking for comments through Sept. 25, 2026. The agency may alter the conditions, decline approval or take a different action after reviewing the record.

If finalized as proposed, the change would give New Hampshire a path to rely on fleet turnover and other plan measures while keeping emissions inspection available as a contingency. The state and federal steps still have to occur in the specified order.
facts: EPA proposes conditional approval rather than an immediate effective repeal.
The proposal depends on separate removal of New Hampshire from the Ozone Transport Region.
A follow-up state implementation plan revision would be due within one year of final conditional approval.
Comments are due Sept. 25, 2026.
uncertainty: The emissions changes are modeled projections rather than observed post-repeal results.
The proposal may change and does not itself alter current driver obligations.
seoTitle: EPA's New Hampshire emissions-test proposal has two conditions
seoDescription: EPA proposes moving New Hampshire vehicle emissions inspections to a contingency measure if two federal air-plan conditions are completed.

headline: Biomedical Science Joins Patent-Bar Degree List
dek: USPTO moved the exact Biomedical Science degree title into Category A, simplifying the technical-training showing for some patent-registration exam applicants.

sources.title: Administrative Updates to the General Requirements Bulletin for Admission to the Examination for Registration to Practice in Patent Cases
General Requirements Bulletin for Admission to the Examination for Registration to Practice in Patent Cases

lead.creator: John F. Williams / Office of Naval Research
lead.rightsBasis: The biomedical laboratory photograph was released by the Office of Naval Research under Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.attribution: John F. Williams / Office of Naval Research, CC BY 2.0
lead.caption: A biomedical engineering student conducts a laboratory experiment with a molecular biologist. USPTO has added the exact Biomedical Science degree title to its Category A list.
lead.alt: A biomedical engineering student and molecular biologist work with laboratory equipment.

charts.caption: USPTO's bulletin provides several ways to demonstrate scientific and technical training; Category A is one route rather than the entire admissions test.
charts.alt: Graphic lists Category A degrees, Category B coursework, Category C practical engineering and Category D other evidence.

charts.caption: After a three-year review, USPTO moved one degree title—Biomedical Science—from Category B to Category A effective Aug. 11.
charts.alt: Graphic shows Biomedical Science moving from Category B to Category A on August 11, 2026.

paragraphs: The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has added Biomedical Science to the Category A degree list used to evaluate scientific and technical training for the patent-registration examination.
The change took effect Aug. 11 and applies to the exact Biomedical Science degree title at the bachelor's, master's or doctoral level under the current General Requirements Bulletin.

Category A lets an applicant establish the technical-training component through a listed degree. It does not automatically admit someone to practice before the USPTO or waive the registration examination and other requirements.
USPTO moved Biomedical Science from Category B after its three-year review of degree titles. The agency says it added 14 degrees to Category A in 2021 and moved one additional degree in this cycle.

The Category A list is not the only route. The bulletin also describes Category B coursework, Category C practical-engineering evidence and a Category D route for other qualifying technical education or experience.

Applicants whose diploma wording differs from a listed title may need transcripts or an equivalency review. The notice says the Category A list is non-exhaustive, but the bulletin's documentary requirements still control each application.

Patent practitioners prepare and prosecute patent applications and represent inventors before the USPTO. The technical-training requirement is separate from state-bar membership, which distinguishes patent attorneys from registered patent agents.

The agency characterizes the update as administrative guidance and says it does not have the force and effect of law. The current bulletin remains the operative source for forms, fees and evidentiary details.

For students and graduates, the practical consequence is narrower paperwork for some applicants with the newly listed degree. It is not a guarantee of examination eligibility, admission or professional licensure.
facts: Biomedical Science moved from Category B to Category A effective Aug. 11, 2026.
The update follows USPTO's three-year review cycle.
Category A addresses scientific and technical training, not every admission requirement.
Other evidence routes remain available under the bulletin.
uncertainty: Degree-title wording and individual records can require transcript or equivalency review.
The notice is guidance; applicants must use the current bulletin and USPTO determination.
seoTitle: Biomedical Science added to USPTO patent-bar Category A list
seoDescription: USPTO moved Biomedical Science into patent-bar Category A, changing how some applicants document technical training for the registration exam.

headline: NRC Rule Changes Comment and Withholding Procedures
dek: The direct final rule revises proprietary-information affidavits, post-promulgation comments, advisory-committee terms and security-eligibility criteria unless adverse comments trigger withdrawal.

sources.title: NRC Modernization: Rulemaking Procedure, Federal Advisory Committee Act Alignment, Access, and Security Requirements
NRC modernization direct final rule, official PDF

lead.creator: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission
lead.rightsBasis: The NRC commission-meeting photograph was released under Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.attribution: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, CC BY 2.0
lead.caption: An NRC public commission meeting on reactor decommissioning. A new direct final rule changes several procedural and information-handling provisions unless adverse comments cause withdrawal.
lead.alt: Nuclear Regulatory Commission members and staff sit at a long table during a public meeting.

charts.caption: The direct final rule groups its updates into four areas: withholding affidavits, post-promulgation comments, advisory committees and security eligibility.
charts.alt: Graphic lists four procedural areas changed by the NRC direct final rule.

charts.caption: The rule is scheduled for Oct. 26, but significant adverse comments received by Sept. 10 would cause NRC to withdraw affected provisions.
charts.alt: Graphic shows September 10 adverse-comment deadline and October 26 scheduled effective date.

paragraphs: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued a direct final rule changing several rulemaking, information-withholding, advisory-committee and security-eligibility procedures.

The rule is scheduled to take effect Oct. 26, 2026. If NRC receives significant adverse comments by 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Sept. 10, the agency says it will publish a withdrawal notice for the affected provisions before that date.

One change removes a requirement that an affidavit supporting the withholding of proprietary information describe the harm that disclosure would cause. Other affidavit and substantiation requirements remain in the regulation.

The rule also revises the commission's self-imposed process for comments received after a rule has been promulgated. NRC describes the change as eliminating a procedure that goes beyond Administrative Procedure Act requirements.

Advisory-committee terminology, charters, appointments and reporting provisions are updated to align with General Services Administration rules issued under the Federal Advisory Committee Act in December 2025.

A fourth set of provisions codifies national-security eligibility criteria from Security Executive Agent Directive 4. NRC says it already uses those criteria internally, so the codification does not establish a new external screening program.

The agency says the rule creates no new obligations for licensees or other external stakeholders and has no cost effect on licensees or the public. Those are NRC's regulatory findings rather than independently measured outcomes.

A direct final rule is used when an agency expects no significant adverse comment. The paired comment process still permits the public to challenge the rule, and qualifying comments can stop the specified provisions from taking effect through this route.
The changes concern process rather than reactor operating standards or a particular license. The codified text and any later withdrawal notice control what becomes effective.
facts: The direct final rule is scheduled to take effect Oct. 26, 2026.
Significant adverse comments are due by Sept. 10 and can trigger withdrawal.
The rule changes withholding affidavits and post-promulgation comment procedures.
It also aligns advisory-committee rules and codifies existing security-eligibility criteria.
uncertainty: NRC may withdraw affected provisions if it receives significant adverse comments.
The agency's no-cost and no-new-obligation findings are its own regulatory assessments.
seoTitle: NRC rule changes withholding, comments and advisory procedures
seoDescription: An NRC direct final rule changes four procedural areas on Oct. 26 unless significant adverse comments by Sept. 10 trigger withdrawal.
